title: The Sword of the Word and the Beauty of Virtue
english: Your thigh, powerful one.

Therefore we say: the faithful man, the self-controlled one, the imitator of God, girds the unyielding Word of God, which is being wielded above every sword, around his thigh, so that he may cut away superfluous desires.
For he who has grasped the honorable marriage and keeps the bed undefiled, has the sword of the Word of God cutting them away.
If 'powerful' here refers to the God-Word or the soul joined to Him, 'thigh' refers to the incarnation, the birth from a woman.
Therefore, preserve this sword while your beauty and your loveliness remain.
And beauty and loveliness are sinlessness, when spoken of the soul; for it did not know sin.
But if spoken of the God-Word, this he says: the beauty and the loveliness of God remain to you, having become man; for you did not change from being the Word and God-Word.
And to each of the rest of the temperate it is said: put on beauty and loveliness from the other virtues, take also temperance, the Word that cuts.
But what kind of sword should we take?
The Word concerning temperance, the Word in general, the one that cuts.
Behold, a wise man is subject to reproof.
This one, progressing and beginning, is so.

But the perfect one is imperturbable; he is not subject to reproof, he does not deviate from the mouth, that is, the Word, the God. 'Make it known to the righteous, and he will add to receiving' (Psalm 112:9); and 'his righteousness is the first argument'.
He entirely possesses what he has argued for himself.
But the truly perfect righteous one is not subject to reproof.
For having watched, he did not seize him, did not strike, did not wound; and thus, at the failure, he grinds the teeth.

And the grinding of teeth often signifies repentance, as also in the Gospel concerning the one bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness 'prepared for the devil and his angels' (Matt 25:41);
'there shall be the weeping and the grinding of teeth' (Matt 8:12).
And the 'there' here again signifies such a condition.
'But the Lord shall laugh at him, for he foresees that his day is coming' (Ps 36:13).
the sinner who shall grind the teeth against the righteous;
for 'he foresees' 'that his day is coming'.
The Lord, foreseeing that his day shall come in which he shall be condemned, shall laugh at the sinner.
But such sayings spoken of God must not be heard in a human-passioned way.
But we take their meaning in a God-befitting way;
for indeed it has been said:
'He who dwells in the heavens shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall sneer at them' (Ps 2:4).
This is not spoken humanly; we do not take it of God in a human-passioned way.
And again in Exodus he says:
'whatsoever I have mocked the Egyptians with' (Ex 10:2).
